titulo: August, the saint, and the week the street belongs to everyone
subtitulo: The month the neighbourhood empties out, the Saturday that feeds your Sunday, the two days a year that belong to one town and nowhere else, and the afternoon a brass band takes the street you were walking down
cena: Quarter past four on a Tuesday in August, twenty-five minutes on foot behind you, a metal shutter down, and the woman in the bar next door watching you read the card taped to it.
decisao: whether the week gets planned around their calendar or yours — the Saturday shop against a Sunday spent walking to a shut grille, and the twenty-five minutes on foot in August that one twenty-second phone call turns into nothing
frasePiso: You will plan a Spanish week around their calendar — the Saturday shop, the shut Tuesday, the street that belongs to a saint. Most visitors spend a fortnight finding it out one shut door at a time.
permissao: August is not a bad month to be in Spain. It is a bad month to rely on one specific address, and ringing first is the whole of the fix. You are allowed to walk into the middle of somebody else's fiesta and stand there watching: the street is the venue, nobody bought a ticket, and the people around you are neighbours, not an audience that paid. And you are allowed to spend a Sunday on a long lunch and a museum, because both of those are open all day.
espelho: Asking why a shop is shut for the whole of August is the bit that reads as odd there. It lands the way 'why is nobody at work on Christmas Day' would land at home — the answer is not a reason, it is a month.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Half a street has metal shutters down on a Tuesday in August, each with a handwritten card taped to the glass, and the bars on the same street are full.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: This corner has gone under, or I have picked the one dead bit of the city to stay in.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: A shop the family owns shuts for the month and everybody in it goes to the coast or back to the village. The card says closed for the holidays and it means the whole of it, not the afternoon — and the opening hours on the map frequently do not know.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Ring before you walk. One question — are you open today — and then carry on in English.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the August the people who live there get: emptier streets, a table anywhere at nine, and every bar, restaurant and museum still running.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not the chains, the department stores, the restaurants or the museums, and not a shop on a street that lives off visitors — none of those shut, and a full shutter row is itself the sign of which kind of street you are standing on.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Sunday lunchtime: the restaurants are full, the bakery has a queue out of the door, and the supermarket four doors along has the grille down.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: It is a holiday nobody told me about and the whole city is shut for it.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Sunday sorts by what the shop sells, not by the hour. Food you eat out is open; food you carry home is not. Declared tourist zones do trade on Sunday, and the residential street your flat is on is not one of them.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Do the big shop on Saturday. Then Sunday is lunch, a walk and whatever has a door open, which is most things.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You spend Sunday the way the neighbours spend it, instead of carrying a rented kitchen's worth of shopping around a street that is not going to open.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in the middle of Madrid or Barcelona, where the declared zone opens seven days a week — walk four streets out of it and the rule comes straight back.

fichasCulturais.sinal: The bank, the town hall and the post office are shut on an ordinary Wednesday, and the town twenty minutes down the road is working normally.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: Something has happened, or there is a strike on that I should know about.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Paid public holidays are capped at fourteen a year: twelve belong to the country and the region and two are chosen by the town hall — usually the patron saint. Those two apply to that municipality and to nowhere else at all.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Ask at the desk on the way in which days are local ones that week, and put the bank and the errands either side of them.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You hear about it the night before rather than at the door, and the day turns into something to go to instead of something that shut the bank.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not for the bars, the restaurants and the terraces. A local holiday is the busiest trading day of their year and every one of them is open, often from breakfast.

fichasCulturais.sinal: A brass band and a few hundred people are coming up the street you wanted, there is no cordon, no ticket and no stage, and everybody around you has stopped walking.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I have wandered into a private thing that is not mine, and I should get out of the way of it.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The street is the venue. The route is published beforehand, it closes while the thing passes, and the people watching are the neighbours — there is no inside to be on the wrong side of.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Stand still, let it pass, ask the person next to you what the day is, and cross behind it rather than through it.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the one afternoon of the fortnight nobody sold you a ticket for, and asking gets it explained to you by somebody who has walked it since they were six.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not on the way to a station or an airport. A route that closes the centre for three hours closes your taxi with it, and that is the morning to go early or go underground.

secoes.titulo: August, and the card taped to the shutter
secoes.corpo: The thing to understand about August is that it is not a slow month, it is an absent one, and only for a particular kind of business: the shop with one family in it. They shut, they put a handwritten card on the glass — CERRADO POR VACACIONES — and they come back in September. Nothing about this is a sign of trouble, and the neighbours all know exactly who is away and where they have gone. What makes it cost you something is not the closure but the listing: opening hours online are very often the ones the shop keeps in March, and a month-long holiday rarely gets typed in anywhere. Hence the rule that is worth more than any sentence in this part — in August, ring before you walk. What does not shut, and this is the half that never gets said: the department stores, the big supermarket chains, the restaurants, the bars, the museums, the galleries and anything on a street that lives off visitors. Sitting inside the month is the fifteenth, la Asunción, a public holiday across the whole country. Plan a supermarket run for the fourteenth and the fifteenth stops mattering. And if you are in the south or the interior, the middle of an August afternoon is not walking time regardless of what anybody is open: two in the afternoon in Seville in August is a taxi, not a stroll, and the shuttered street at four is partly the reason the evening starts at nine.

secoes.titulo: Two ranges on the card, not one
secoes.corpo: A small shop's day has a hole in the middle of it. Roughly: open around ten, down at half one or two, back up at half four or five, and then trading until eight or half eight — which is why the horario card by the door has two ranges printed on it and why reading only the first one is how people end up outside a locked chemist at three. This is commercial, not biological: almost nobody is asleep. The country is at lunch, which is the big meal, and lunch takes a proper hour and a half. What ignores the hole entirely: El Corte Inglés and the other department stores, Mercadona, Lidl, Carrefour, Zara and the chains generally, every restaurant (it is their peak), and the museums. So the practical shape of an afternoon is that the errand goes before half one or after five, and the middle belongs to eating and to anything with a roof and air conditioning. One more card worth knowing by sight: HORARIO DE VERANO, summer opening hours, which is a different and usually shorter timetable taped over the normal one. If two cards are on the glass, the seasonal one is the one that counts.

secoes.titulo: Fourteen days, and the two that belong to one town
secoes.corpo: Spanish labour law caps paid public holidays at fourteen a year, and it says explicitly that two of them are local. That single sentence explains almost everything odd you will meet in a calendar here. Nine or so are national, a few more are set by the region, and then the town hall of the place you happen to be standing in picks two — nearly always the patron saint of the town or of the neighbourhood. The consequence for a visitor is the one nobody warns you about: a Wednesday can be completely shut in one town and a normal working day in the town twenty minutes down the road, and no national calendar you look up will show it. What actually closes is the official layer — banks, town halls, post offices, many chemists, most small shops, some museums. What does not close is hospitality: a local holiday is one of the best trading days of the year for the bars and the restaurants, and they open early for it. The move is trivial and it is the whole point of this part: ask at the hotel desk, on arrival, which days that week are local ones, and put the bank and the paperwork on either side of them. Holy Week works on the same logic with a moving date, since it is tied to Easter and shifts every year — the useful thing to know about it is that in a lot of towns the calendar is less disrupted than the street map is.

exemplos.pt: mah-NYAH-nah ehs FYEHS-tah — is tomorrow a public holiday? Three words, asked the night before
ehs FYEHS-tah loh-KAHL — 👂 it's a local holiday. Meaning here, and not in the next town

secoes.corpo: A procession — a patron saint going out, a Holy Week brotherhood, a neighbourhood fiesta with a band — uses the street as the venue. There is no gate, no ticket, no seating and no inside: the route is published in advance by the town hall and the local press, the road closes while the thing passes, and the crowd is made of the people who live on it. Three small pieces of etiquette cover you completely. Stand still while it goes by rather than walking across the front of it. Cross behind, not through. And if you want to know what it is, ask the person next to you, because being asked is a small pleasure for somebody who has walked in it since they were a child. The one operational fact worth planning around is that a route through the centre can shut it to traffic for hours, taxis included, so a station or airport run on a fiesta afternoon goes early or goes underground. Finally, the other end of the year, which is the piece most British visitors have backwards: the Canary Islands run an inverted season, and November to February is their best and busiest stretch, while the Balearics are a May to October proposition. Booking the Canaries for August and the Balearics for January is the single most common way to get the wrong island at the wrong time.
